theme: AI at Work: Start Where You Are
title: Set the Tone
titleHtml: Your team's AI use starts with your tone.
tagline: Framing AI as a leadership responsibility.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for Vanderbilt managers: learn why safe AI adoption on a team is led, how to model one safe first use, and how to talk about AI with your team in a way that invites curiosity.
heroLead: Teams take their AI cue from their manager, and silence reads as an answer. Today you set the tone on purpose, starting with one safe use you model yourself.
objectives: Name the three signals a team reads from its manager about AI: permission, safety, curiosity
Choose one green-light task from your own week and model it for your team
Open a team conversation about AI that is honest about limits and free of hype
missionTie: Defining the great university of the 21st Century takes managers who make safe AI use normal on their own teams, and Exceptional Core Operations grows one team at a time as they do.

agenda.d: What your team reads from your silence, your hype, and your curiosity.
The traffic light, and picking a first use your team can watch you run.
Words that invite experiments and keep the guardrails visible.

manifesto: Model one green-light use for your team and say out loud what is in bounds.

sections.headline: Your team reads three signals from you.
sections.lead: Teams read three signals from their manager about AI: permission, safety, and curiosity. They read them from what you say and do, and silence gets read too. This section covers how to set all three on purpose, starting with saying out loud what is allowed.
sections.group: In pairs: what tone has your team read from you about AI so far, on purpose or by accident? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Write one line: what tone has your team read from you about AI so far, on purpose or by accident?

deeper.title: The three signals, decoded
deeper.body: Each signal has a telltale question behind it. Permission: has my manager ever said out loud that we may use AI here? Safety: could I state the boundary in one sentence if a new hire asked? Curiosity: when someone mentions an experiment, does the manager lean in or change the subject? Teams answer these from small moments, like what you laughed at, what you ignored, and what you asked about. A tone audit starts there.
steps: Answer the three questions the way your team would, based only on what they have watched you do and say.
Pick the weakest signal and script one sentence that makes it explicit at your next team meeting.

card.text: A team's AI behavior mirrors its manager's signals. They listen for three things: permission (may we?), safety (what is in bounds?), and curiosity (does trying count?). When all three are clear, safe experiments start.

interaction.context: McKinsey's Superagency research found employees readier for AI than their leaders assume; the pace of adoption is set higher up. Your team is probably not waiting on training or news coverage. They are waiting to hear from you what is allowed and what is smart.
interaction.discuss: Where did your own read on AI come from: a manager, a policy page, or the news? What does that say about what your team is reading from you right now?
interaction.q: Quick check: a manager has never mentioned AI to the team. What does the team most likely conclude?

opts.t: AI is fine here as long as nobody asks
opts.why: Some will quietly assume that, with zero guardrails. Silence produces shadow use by the bold and total avoidance by the careful.

opts.t: The topic is off limits until the manager raises it
opts.why: Most people default to caution and wait. Meanwhile a few experiment unguided, which is the riskiest mix a team can have.

opts.t: Nothing; teams form AI habits on their own
opts.why: Habits form around what the manager permits and models. McKinsey found staff readier than leaders assume, which makes your signal the one they wait on.

sections.headline: Model the first green light.
sections.lead: The shared traffic light keeps this simple. Green, public or generic information: go. Yellow, internal work: approved VU tools only. Red, private information about people: never. Pick a boring green chore and let your team watch you run it, fixes and all.
sections.group: In pairs: name one green-light chore from your own week you could model for your team this month. 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Name one green-light chore from your own week you could model for your team this month.

deeper.title: When the light is hard to call
deeper.body: Real chores mix information, and the most sensitive piece decides the light for the whole task. A job posting built from the public description is green; paste in notes from the finalist interviews and the same task turns red. That gives you a second move to model: strip the chore. Remove the internal or personal specifics, run the generic skeleton on green, and add the sensitive parts back yourself afterward.
steps: List two chores from your week that feel yellow or red, and find the green skeleton inside each by removing specifics.
Write the exact input you would give the tool for one of them, then reread it for anything internal or personal.

interaction.intro: Your team will bring you cases exactly like these. Call each one before you have to answer theirs.
interaction.passMsg: You can call the light. Model green ones openly, route yellow through approved VU tools, and hold the red line every time.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The light follows the information: public or generic is green, internal work is yellow inside approved VU tools, and private information about people is always red.

items.q: You want AI to draft a first version of a job posting using only the public role description.
items.why: Public information, generic task. This is a perfect first use to model: low stakes, visible, and easy for the team to copy.

items.q: An analyst asks to summarize an internal budget planning document with an AI tool.
items.why: Internal content is yellow: fine inside approved VU tools, off limits anywhere else. Your answer teaches the team where the boundary runs.

items.q: A coordinator wants AI help drafting feedback about a struggling employee, details pasted in.
items.why: Private information about a person is red, always. AI can help with generic feedback structures; the specifics about a person never go in.

sections.headline: Say what you tried and what is in bounds.
sections.lead: The team conversation that works is plain: here is what I tried, here is what is in bounds, and I want to hear what you try. Hype invites eye rolls, and fear drives experiments underground. Build the version you would say at your next team meeting.

deeper.title: Keeping the conversation alive
deeper.body: One good conversation sets the tone; a small ritual keeps it. Reserve two minutes of each team meeting for one AI share, with the same beats you modeled: what I tried, what it did well, what I fixed. Expect silence for the first week or two, and fill it with another small use of your own rather than pressing anyone. Once results get shared out loud, checking becomes a habit the team keeps visible for itself.
steps: Add a standing two-minute item called one AI share to your team agenda for the next month.
Prepare two of your own shares in advance so early silence never stalls the ritual.
When the first volunteer shares, ask what they fixed; that question keeps the editor habit in view.

interaction.intro: Your team meeting, five minutes on the agenda. Choose how you open and what you invite.

opts.t: AI is coming for every job, so we all need to get on board fast.
opts.coach: Fear opens mouths and closes minds. People nod along, then avoid the topic and hide whatever they try.

opts.t: Leadership wants us using AI more, so have a look when you get a chance.
opts.coach: Permission by memo. It hands the tone to a distant voice and gives nobody a picture of what safe use looks like.

opts.t: I used AI to draft the job posting this week. Here is what it did well and what I fixed.
opts.coach: A modeled green-light use, limits included. Showing your own work grants permission and teaches the guardrails in one move.

opts.t: Come to me first before anyone touches an AI tool.
opts.coach: A bottleneck reads as a warning. Experiments stop, or they continue quietly where you can never coach them.

opts.t: Try it if you like; just be sensible about what you put in.
opts.coach: Sensible means something different to everyone. Without the traffic light, each person draws their own line.

opts.t: Pick one green-light chore, try it, and bring what happened to next week's meeting.
opts.coach: A specific invitation with the guardrail built in. Sharing results out loud turns one experiment into a team habit.

heads.strong: A tone that travels. The team saw a real use, heard real limits, and got a specific invitation to try.
heads.mid: Permission was granted and never shaped. A few will try things; most will wait for a clearer signal.
heads.weak: The room went quiet. People heard pressure or a warning, and the experiments that happen next will be invisible ones.

reactions.strong: Within two weeks, three people bring green-light experiments to the team meeting, including one you would never have thought of. The traffic light gets quoted back to you, which is how you know it stuck.
reactions.mid: A month later, one adventurous person uses AI regularly and nobody else has started. Adoption became a personality trait on your team instead of a team practice.
reactions.weak: Weeks later you learn someone has been pasting internal documents into a free tool at home. The conversation that would have prevented it never happened.

recap.q: What do teams read most closely to decide how they will use AI?
opts: Their manager's signals: permission, safety, curiosity
recap.why: Policy sets the outer boundary; daily behavior forms around the local manager. Your signals are the ones the team actually acts on.

recap.q: An analyst wants to summarize an internal planning doc with AI. Your call?
opts: Ask them to wait until next quarter
recap.why: Internal content is yellow: fine inside approved VU tools, off limits everywhere else. The information decides the light every time.

recap.q: What makes a manager's first modeled AI use land with the team?
opts: It is a boring green chore shown honestly, fixes included
recap.why: A visible, low-stakes use with its flaws shown gives the team permission and the checking habit together. Impressive demos mostly create distance.

recapMsgs.high: You have all three pieces. Model the green-light chore this week.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Revisit the traffic light, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you commit.

capstone.headline: One green light, modeled out loud.
capstone.lead: Pick the chore you will model and the moment the team hears about it. Nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: The green-light chore you will model, and where the team hears about it.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. drafting the job posting; share at Tuesday staff meeting
capstone.practiceLabel: Which move do you lead with?

practices.name: Model it live
practices.move: Run one green-light chore with AI, then show the team what it produced and what you fixed.

practices.name: Teach the traffic light
practices.move: Walk the team through green, yellow, and red with one real example of each from your own work.

practices.name: The open invitation
practices.move: Invite everyone to try one green-light chore and bring what happened to the next team meeting.

whens.out: The move happens this week, on the team agenda by Friday.
The move opens your next team meeting, first item, before status updates.
The move happens within two weeks, on the agenda today so it cannot slide.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did your team try once they saw you go first?

closing.headline: Model the chore this week.
closing.lead: You know the signals your team reads, and you have a green light picked and the words to open with. Tuesday and Thursday carry the same theme to every staff member.

facilitator.audience: Vanderbilt people managers and team leads in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; January opens the AI at Work theme with the new calendar year, and this is many managers' first AI session.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did you model the chore on your card? What did the team say or try afterward? What is the next green light you will point at?' Count of modeled first uses is the Level 3 metric for the month.

s1.title: The tone you set
s1.purpose: Establish that team AI behavior mirrors the manager's signals: permission, safety, curiosity.
s1.say: New year, new theme. McKinsey went looking for what holds AI back at work and found it was rarely the employees; most are readier than their leaders assume. The pace gets set by the person in front of the team, which is you, and silence sets it too. Say nothing and the careful people freeze while the bold ones experiment with zero guardrails. So today we set the tone on purpose.
facilitate: Read the tone rule card aloud, then let the context on screen land; the live room gets the framing, no quiz.
Run the discussion: where did your own read on AI come from? Take two or three voices before you weigh in.
Run the breakout: what tone has your team read so far, 90 seconds each way.

ask.q: What tone do you suspect your own team has read from you so far?
expect: A few who have been enthusiastic without guardrails
ask.respond: Both are common and both are fixable. The next two sections give you the model and the words.

s1.debrief: Permission, safety, curiosity. When the team can answer all three without asking you, the tone is set.
s1.watchFor: Managers who feel behind because they have never used AI themselves. Name it early: this month assumes zero experience, and going first with a small chore counts double.
s1.transition: The tone gets set fastest by what you model. Here is how to pick the first use.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; ask for one word in chat describing the team's current tone.

s2.title: Model one safe use
s2.purpose: Install the traffic light and have every manager pick one green-light chore to model.
s2.say: The traffic light is the whole safety model, and it travels because it is short. Green is public or generic information: go. Yellow is internal work: approved VU tools only. Red is private information about people: never. Your first modeled use should be a boring green chore, because boring is copyable.
facilitate: Run Green, yellow, or red? live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After the red case, pause: ask why a kind intention leaves the light red.
Run the breakout: one green-light chore from your own week.

ask.q: Why should your first modeled use be boring rather than impressive?
expect: Low stakes means mistakes teach cheaply
ask.respond: Right. The goal is a team full of small safe experiments, and those start from a chore everyone recognizes.

s2.debrief: The information decides the light every time. Green goes, yellow stays inside approved VU tools, red never goes in.
s2.watchFor: Managers inventing edge cases to postpone action. Park edge cases in chat for the tough-questions bank and bring the room back to their one green chore.
s2.transition: You have the use. Now the team needs to hear about it in the right tone.
s2.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the debrief question.

s3.title: The team conversation
s3.purpose: Build an opening and an invitation that grant permission with the guardrails visible.
s3.say: Last piece: the words. Oversell this and people tune out. Scare them and the experiments go underground, which is where the real risk lives. What works is plain talk: what I tried, what is in bounds, what I want to hear back. Let's build yours.
facilitate: Run Open the AI conversation; two minutes to make both choices and run it.
Ask one volunteer to read their outcome aloud, weak or strong.
Point at the pattern: a modeled use plus a specific invitation with the guardrail built in.

ask.q: What makes 'be sensible about what you put in' a weak guardrail?
expect: It pushes the judgment onto the least informed person
ask.respond: Exactly. The traffic light exists so nobody has to improvise the boundary. Give the rule, then invite the experiment.

s3.debrief: The strong conversation has a shape: I tried this, here is the light system, bring me what you try.
s3.watchFor: Managers drafting a policy memo in their heads. Keep it spoken and small; the tone lives in the meeting, and the memo can follow.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you build your own card.
s3.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it real. One green-light chore from your own week, one moment where the team hears about it. Pick the move, pick the window, build the card, and copy it somewhere you will see it before Friday. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: You leave with a tone to set and a chore to model. Tomorrow's Take-Off Tuesday is the hands-on session: every staff member picks one safe AI use case and runs it, so send your whole team. Thursday's Thrive Thursday builds adaptability, the skill of leading through the ambiguity that arrives with any new tool. And if you want more depth, this month's LinkedIn Learning course is Generative AI for Business Leaders with Kian Katanforoosh, and the navigators are hosting a First-AI-Win sandbox session for anyone who wants a guided first run.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: A manager shares a story with private details about a named employee's AI mistake
contingencies.then: Protect them warmly and immediately: 'Hold that. Roles, never names.' The lesson travels fine without the person attached.

contingencies.if: The room splits between AI enthusiasts and skeptics
contingencies.then: Give each side one sentence, then point at the traffic light: it gives enthusiasts a lane and skeptics a boundary, and it asks both for the same small move.

toughQuestions.q: I have never used an AI tool myself. How can I set the tone?
toughQuestions.a: Start where you are; that is the month's theme. Pick one green-light chore, try it this week, and model it honestly, fixes and all. A manager learning out loud sets a better tone than an expert performing. The navigator-led First-AI-Win sandbox session is a guided place to do that first run.

toughQuestions.q: What if someone on my team is already pasting internal content into free tools?
toughQuestions.a: Treat it as a signal of appetite, and address the boundary without shaming the experiment. Teach the traffic light, route the yellow work into approved VU tools, and thank them for surfacing it. Curiosity is fuel you want; it just needs the guardrails.

toughQuestions.q: Is AI adoption really my job? We have IT and a policy for that.
toughQuestions.a: Policy and platforms set the outer boundary; daily behavior forms around what you permit and model. Your team builds its habits around you long before anyone reads a policy page. That is why this month treats adoption as a leadership responsibility, and why the ask is one modeled chore, small enough for any calendar.
